units.title: Security Goals and Classical Ciphers
topics: Seeing the ciphers: machines, frequencies and keyspaces

sections.title: Seeing the ciphers: machines, frequencies and keyspaces

summary: Security services are confidentiality, integrity, authentication, non-repudiation and availability; attacks are passive or active; security must rest on the key (Kerckhoffs).
Substitution ciphers (Caesar, affine, Vigenère, Playfair, Hill) and transposition ciphers (rail fence) are all breakable by exploiting language structure or linearity.
Hill encryption is C = K·P mod 26 and needs gcd(det K, 26) = 1; here det K = 441 ≡ 25 (mod 26), and ACT encrypts to POH.
A one-time pad is perfectly secret but impractical; key reuse destroys it.

topics: The Euclidean and extended Euclidean algorithms
Primitive roots and the discrete logarithm

Seeing the arithmetic: portraits, clocks, cycles and chains

sections.title: The Euclidean and extended Euclidean algorithms
Primitive roots and the discrete logarithm
Why the arithmetic is feasible and the inverse is hard
Seeing the arithmetic: portraits, clocks, cycles and chains

summary: a mod n arithmetic is closed under + − ×; an inverse exists iff gcd(a, n) = 1; the extended Euclidean algorithm finds it (240·(−9) + 46·47 = 2; 7⁻¹ ≡ 15 mod 26).
φ(p) = p − 1, φ(pq) = (p − 1)(q − 1); Fermat a^(p−1) ≡ 1; Euler a^φ(n) ≡ 1; CRT combines congruences (x ≡ 2, 3, 2 mod 3, 5, 7 gives 23).
Square-and-multiply makes huge powers cheap; Miller–Rabin finds primes where the Fermat test is fooled by Carmichael numbers such as 561.
Primitive roots and the hard discrete log underlie Diffie–Hellman and ElGamal.

units.title: Symmetric Ciphers - Feistel, DES, AES and Modes of Operation
topics: Block and stream ciphers, confusion and diffusion
Seeing symmetric ciphers: hardware, rounds and chaining

sections.title: Block and stream ciphers, confusion and diffusion
Seeing symmetric ciphers: hardware, rounds and chaining

summary: Confusion (substitution) and diffusion (permutation) are combined over many rounds; a Feistel network's rounds are invertible even if F is not.
DES: 64-bit block, 56-bit key, 16 rounds, 8 S-boxes; exhaustive search takes 20.0 hours at 10¹² keys/s, so it is obsolete; 3DES is deprecated.
AES: 128-bit block, 10/12/14 rounds of SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey over GF(2⁸); {57}•{83} = {c1}; verified here against the FIPS-197 vector.
ECB leaks patterns (equal blocks → equal ciphertext); CBC needs a random IV; CTR needs a unique nonce; GCM adds authentication and is the modern default.

units.title: Public-Key Cryptography - RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ElGamal and ECC
topics: Seeing public-key cryptography: pioneers, keys and curves

sections.title: Seeing public-key cryptography: pioneers, keys and curves

summary: Public-key cryptography removes the shared-secret problem: n users need n key pairs instead of n(n − 1)/2, and it is used to exchange symmetric keys (hybrid encryption).
RSA: n = pq, d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n), c = mᵉ mod n, m = cᵈ mod n; the example n = 3233, d = 2753 encrypts 65 to 2790; real RSA needs OAEP/PSS padding and ≥ 2048-bit keys.
Diffie–Hellman agrees gᵃᵇ mod p and needs authentication against man-in-the-middle; ElGamal encrypts with a fresh k.
Elliptic curves give the same security with far smaller keys; the example curve has a point of order 19.

units.title: Hash Functions, MACs, Digital Signatures and PKI
summary: A cryptographic hash is preimage-, second-preimage- and collision-resistant with avalanche; MD5 and SHA-1 are broken, SHA-256 and SHA-3 are secure.
Birthday bound: collisions appear after about 1.1774·√N messages: 23 people give 0.5073 for N = 365; a 64-bit digest falls after about 5,056,894,494 messages.
HMAC(K, m) = H((K ⊕ opad) ‖ H((K ⊕ ipad) ‖ m)) authenticates with a shared key; checked here against RFC 4231.
Digital signatures (RSA-PSS, ECDSA, Ed25519) give authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation; reusing the ECDSA nonce reveals the key.
X.509 certificates, CAs and chains of trust bind keys to identities; revocation by CRL/OCSP; Nepal's CCA licenses CAs under the ETA 2063.
Passwords need salts and slow hashes (Argon2id, bcrypt).

units.title: Authentication and Secure Network Protocols
topics: Seeing the protocols: tickets, handshakes and tunnels

sections.title: Seeing the protocols: tickets, handshakes and tunnels

summary: Authentication uses what you know, have or are; protocols need nonces or timestamps against replay and authenticated key exchange against man-in-the-middle; TOTP = HMAC over a time counter.
Kerberos issues a TGT then service tickets; passwords never travel, but clocks and the KDC are critical.
TLS 1.3 completes its handshake in one round trip with ephemeral DH (forward secrecy): time to first byte at 80 ms RTT is 240 ms against 320 ms for TLS 1.2.
IPsec ESP in tunnel mode adds 64 bytes to a 1400-byte packet; AH is rarely used; IKEv2 sets up SAs.
PGP uses a hybrid signed-and-encrypted design with a web of trust; SSH uses host and user keys.

units.title: Network and System Security - Firewalls, IDS, VPN and Wireless
topics: Key management and a security checklist
Seeing network defences: walls, zones, sensors and radios

sections.title: Key management and a security checklist
Seeing network defences: walls, zones, sensors and radios

summary: Firewalls enforce ordered, first-match, default-deny rules; types range from packet filters to NGFWs and WAFs; DMZs isolate public servers.
IDS/IPS use signatures or anomaly detection; with a rare attack (0.1%), a 99%-detecting, 1%-false-alarm IDS gives alerts that are about 91.0% false.
VPNs tunnel traffic with IPsec, TLS or WireGuard; zero-trust assumes no trusted inside.
WPA3 (SAE) replaces WPA2-PSK; WEP is broken; enterprise Wi-Fi uses 802.1X.
Key management (secure generation, storage in HSMs/keystores, rotation, envelope encryption) decides whether the cryptography protects anything.

units.title: Malware, Intruders, Steganography, Network Management Security and Cyber Law
topics: Secure Electronic Transaction and the dual signature
Cloud, mobile and e-mail security in brief

sections.title: Secure Electronic Transaction and the dual signature
Cloud, mobile and e-mail security in brief

summary: Malware types differ by host dependence and replication; defence is layered (patching, least privilege, detection, backups).
Intruders are masqueraders, misfeasors or clandestine users; password strength is a matter of random length and slow salted hashing.
Steganography hides existence, cryptography hides content; LSB embedding is simple, invisible and fragile.
SNMPv1/v2c use clear-text community strings; SNMPv3 adds authentication, privacy and access control.
The dual signature links PI and OI while hiding each from the wrong party.
Law and ethics define what a security professional may do; in Nepal the Electronic Transactions Act, 2063 is the core statute.
